jobs/recall: In attention over the encoder, the decoder's query, q, scored each encoder state with a dot product: how far that state's arrow reaches along q.
jobs/blend: Then the same arrows were shrunk by their weights and added up into the context vector.
jobs/tug: So each arrow has two jobs. Turn suis toward q, and its score climbs. But what suis hands over turns with it.
jobs/clash: What makes a word easy to find need not be what it should hand over. One arrow cannot serve both.
jobs/daniluk: In 2017, Michał Daniluk and colleagues hit this in a language model: one vector had to predict the next word, be scored, and be handed over. One vector per job worked better.
lookup/dict: A Python dictionary keeps two such jobs apart: each entry pairs a key, to look it up by, with a value, to get back.
lookup/exact: Ask for cats, and the key cats matches: out comes its value, two, zero. The value can be anything.
lookup/names: Attention borrows the names. A query asks, the keys are what it is matched against, and the values are what come back.
lookup/soft: But the match is soft: every key matches a little, by its dot product with the query, and back comes a blend of all the values.
lookup/vaswani: In 2017, Ashish Vaswani and colleagues at Google defined attention in these terms: a query and key-value pairs, mapped to a weighted sum of the values.
make/maps: So give each token, x, three arrows of its own, each made by a learned matrix that every token shares: W, marked Q, K or V for its job.
make/q: The query is W Q times x, one dot product per row: three, one. The arrow turns and stretches.
make/k: The key, k, is W K times x: one, minus one.
make/v: And the value, v, is W V times x: minus one, two. Three arrows, each free to point its own way.
make/rows: Each row is dotted with x to make one entry. So a matrix has one row per entry it makes, and one column per entry of x.
make/d: Real tokens are much longer. Write d for how many numbers a token has.
make/dk: And d k for how many a query has. A key has as many, to be dotted with it. So W Q is d k by d.
make/big: Vaswani's model had a d of five hundred twelve and a d k of sixty four, so W Q is sixty four by five hundred twelve.
match/ask: Back to a sentence: cats like fish. Each token has its key, made by W K. Fish asks with its query: zero, one, straight up.
match/score: Its query is dotted with every key, its own included. As q points straight up, each score is how high a key reaches. Cats' key scores two.
match/others: Like's key lies at a right angle to q, so it scores zero. Fish's own key reaches one.
match/weights: Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to one: cats gets about two thirds.
match/mix: Fish's output blends the values by those weights: shrink each, then add them tip to tail. It lands near cats' value.
match/roles: So the query and the keys decide how much each token counts, and the values what it brings: two jobs, two arrows.
